terms.compare: Like the secret words only basketball players use — "pick and roll", "and-one".
terms.meaning: Special words used by people in one field.
terms.more: Every underlined word in this app is jargon. Tap it any time. Nobody remembers all of them on day one.
terms.example: Your IT colleagues say "DNS", "SSL", "cron" — that's jargon.

terms.compare: Like a very fast, very obedient office clerk.
terms.meaning: A machine that follows instructions to store and process information.
terms.more: Every computer has a processor (CPU) that thinks, memory (RAM) for short-term work, and storage (disk) for keeping files.
terms.example: Your office PC, your server and even your iPhone are all computers.

terms.compare: Like the national road network connecting every town.
terms.meaning: A giant worldwide network of connected computers.
terms.more: The internet is the roads. The web (websites) is just one kind of traffic on those roads. Email and video calls are other kinds.
terms.example: Your agency's website reaches the public through the internet.

terms.compare: Like a barangay where houses are connected by small streets.
terms.meaning: Two or more computers connected so they can share information.
terms.more: A LAN (local area network) is the network inside your office. The internet is a network of networks.
terms.example: The switches and cables you manage form your office network.

terms.compare: Like a customer ordering at a restaurant.
terms.meaning: The device or program that asks for something.
terms.more: Your browser is a client. It sends a request and waits for a response from a server.
terms.example: When staff open the agency site on their phones, each phone is a client.

terms.compare: Like the restaurant kitchen that prepares and serves the food.
terms.meaning: A computer (or program) that waits for requests and sends back answers.
terms.more: "Server" can mean the physical machine OR the software that answers (like IIS or Apache). Servers usually run 24/7.
terms.example: Your Windows server that hosts the WordPress site is a server.

terms.compare: Like a waiter that takes your order and brings back the food.
terms.meaning: The app you use to view websites, like Safari or Chrome.
terms.more: The browser sends HTTP requests, receives HTML/CSS/JS files and draws them into a page.
terms.example: You test the agency site in Safari, Chrome and Edge.

terms.compare: Like a house's exact street address.
terms.meaning: A number that identifies a device on a network, like 192.168.1.10.
terms.more: IPv4 looks like 203.0.113.5 (four numbers 0–255). IPv6 is longer, like 2001:db8::1. Private IPs (192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) only work inside your office.
terms.example: Your server has a fixed IP so the router always knows where to send web traffic.

terms.compare: Like a business name on a signboard instead of the GPS coordinates.
terms.meaning: An easy-to-remember name for a website, like nrcp.dost.gov.ph.
terms.more: Domains are read right to left: .ph (country) → .gov (government) → dost → nrcp. You rent them from a registrar.
terms.example: Your agency's website address is its domain.

terms.compare: Like the phone's contacts app: you tap a name, it finds the number.
terms.meaning: The system that turns a domain name into an IP address.
terms.more: Your device asks a DNS resolver, which asks other DNS servers until it finds the A record (IP) for the name. Answers are cached for a time called TTL.
terms.example: If the site 'can't be found' after a server move, DNS records may still point to the old IP.

terms.compare: Like a full mailing address: city, street, house number, room.
terms.meaning: The complete address of one thing on the web.
terms.more: Example: https://example.gov.ph/news/index.php?id=5 — protocol, domain, path, and query.
terms.example: Each WordPress post has its own URL (permalink).

terms.compare: Like the standard order form used between customer and kitchen.
terms.meaning: The set of rules browsers and servers use to talk.
terms.more: HyperText Transfer Protocol. A request has a method (GET, POST), a path and headers. A response has a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error).
terms.example: When you see '404' on the site, that's an HTTP status code.

terms.compare: Like sending your order in a sealed envelope instead of a postcard.
terms.meaning: HTTP with encryption, so nobody in between can read or change it.
terms.more: The S means Secure. It uses TLS/SSL certificates. iPhones need HTTPS for offline web apps.
terms.example: The padlock icon on your agency site means HTTPS is working.

terms.compare: Like an official ID card plus a lockable box.
terms.meaning: The technology (and certificate) that makes HTTPS secure.
terms.more: SSL is the old name; TLS is the modern version. A certificate proves the site is really yours and must be renewed before it expires.
terms.example: If the certificate expires, visitors see a scary warning — set a renewal reminder.

terms.compare: Like the rules of a formal meeting: who speaks first, how to end.
terms.meaning: An agreed set of rules for how computers communicate.
terms.more: HTTP, FTP, DNS and SMTP (email) are all protocols.
terms.example: Choosing SFTP instead of FTP is choosing a safer protocol.

terms.compare: Like placing an order.
terms.meaning: A message from a client asking a server for something.
terms.more: An HTTP request includes a method (GET to read, POST to send), a URL and headers.
terms.example: Every page view on your site starts with a request.

terms.compare: Like the food the kitchen sends back, with a note saying 'Here you go'.
terms.meaning: The server's answer to a request.
terms.more: Includes a status code (like 200), headers and a body (the HTML, image, etc.).
terms.example: A slow response time means the server is taking long to cook the page.

terms.compare: Like a traffic enforcer pointing cars to the right road.
terms.meaning: A device that sends data between networks.
terms.more: Your office router connects the LAN to the internet and decides where each packet goes.
terms.example: Port forwarding on the router sends web traffic to your server.

terms.compare: Like sending a long letter as many numbered postcards.
terms.meaning: A small piece of data sent across a network.
terms.more: Big files are split into packets, sent separately, and put back together at the other end.
terms.example: Packet loss on a network makes websites and calls feel slow.

terms.compare: Like the company that built the road to your house.
terms.meaning: The company that connects you to the internet (e.g. PLDT, Globe, Converge).
terms.more: Your ISP gives you a public IP and carries your traffic.
terms.example: If the whole office has no internet, the ISP may be down.

terms.compare: Like renting a stall in a mall for your store.
terms.meaning: A place (a server) where your website's files live and are served.
terms.more: Can be your own server (self-hosted, like yours) or a rented one from a company (shared, VPS, cloud).
terms.example: Your agency self-hosts on a Windows server.

terms.compare: Like talking to yourself in the mirror.
terms.meaning: A name that means 'this same computer'.
terms.more: localhost always points to 127.0.0.1. Great for testing a site before it goes public.
terms.example: With XAMPP you open http://localhost/ to see your test site.

terms.compare: Like the numbered doors of a big building — each door for a different service.
terms.meaning: A number that says which program on a computer should get the message.
terms.more: Web uses 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS). MySQL uses 3306. RDP uses 3389. One IP, many ports.
terms.example: If Apache won't start in XAMPP, another app may already be using port 80.

terms.compare: Like the kitchen staff who actually cook and plate the orders.
terms.meaning: Software that receives HTTP requests and sends back web pages.
terms.more: Examples: IIS, Apache, Nginx. It finds the right file or runs PHP, then sends the result.
terms.example: Your Windows server runs a web server program to serve WordPress.

terms.compare: Like a kitchen brand made by Microsoft.
terms.meaning: Microsoft's web server software, built into Windows Server.
terms.more: Managed with IIS Manager. Sites live in folders like C:\inetpub\wwwroot. Can run PHP with FastCGI.
terms.example: Your WordPress site may be served by IIS on the Windows server.

terms.compare: Like another popular kitchen brand, free and open to everyone.
terms.meaning: A free, very popular web server program.
terms.more: Configured with httpd.conf and .htaccess files. Included in XAMPP.
terms.example: WordPress permalinks on Apache use the .htaccess file.

terms.compare: Like a 'kitchen-in-a-box' kit you can set up at home.
terms.meaning: A free package that installs Apache, MySQL (MariaDB), PHP and more on your PC.
terms.more: X = any OS, A = Apache, M = MariaDB/MySQL, P = PHP, P = Perl. Files go in C:\xampp\htdocs.
terms.example: Use XAMPP to test WordPress changes safely before touching the real server.

terms.compare: Like who holds which keys in the office.
terms.meaning: Rules saying who can read, change or run a file or folder.
terms.more: On Windows these are NTFS permissions (Read, Write, Modify, Full control). Too much = unsafe, too little = errors.
terms.example: WordPress needs write permission on wp-content/uploads to upload images.

terms.compare: Like one sheet of paper or one document.
terms.meaning: A single saved piece of information on a computer.
terms.more: Files have names and extensions (.php, .html, .jpg) that hint what's inside.
terms.example: wp-config.php is a file that holds WordPress settings.

terms.compare: Like a folder in a filing cabinet.
terms.meaning: A container that holds files and other folders.
terms.more: Also called a directory. Folders inside folders make a path like C:\inetpub\wwwroot\wp-content.
terms.example: Themes live in the wp-content/themes folder.

terms.compare: Like a super-organized filing cabinet with labeled drawers.
terms.meaning: An organized place to store data so it's easy to find and update.
terms.more: Data is in tables (like spreadsheets) with rows and columns. Programs talk to it using SQL.
terms.example: WordPress keeps all posts, pages and users in a database.

terms.compare: Like one particular brand of filing cabinet.
terms.meaning: A popular database program. WordPress uses it (or its twin, MariaDB).
terms.more: Listens on port 3306. Managed with phpMyAdmin or command line.
terms.example: Back up the MySQL database before every WordPress update.

terms.compare: Like the exact sentences you say to the filing-cabinet clerk.
terms.meaning: The language used to ask a database for data or change it.
terms.more: Structured Query Language. Example: SELECT post_title FROM wp_posts WHERE post_status='publish';
terms.example: In phpMyAdmin you can run SQL queries.

terms.compare: Like the cook who reads the recipe and prepares a dish fresh for each customer.
terms.meaning: A programming language that runs on the server and builds web pages.
terms.more: PHP runs before the page is sent. The visitor only receives the resulting HTML. WordPress is written in PHP.
terms.example: Files like functions.php in your theme are PHP.

terms.compare: Like the skeleton (or the walls and rooms) of a house.
terms.meaning: The language that gives a web page its structure: headings, paragraphs, images, links.
terms.more:
HyperText Markup Language. It uses tags like

and

. It is not a programming language — it describes, it doesn't calculate.
terms.example: WordPress turns your post into HTML before sending it.

terms.compare: Like the clothes, paint and decoration.
terms.meaning: The language that controls how a page looks: colors, fonts, spacing, layout.
terms.more: Cascading Style Sheets. Rules look like: h1 { color: green; }
terms.example: Your WordPress theme's style.css controls the site's look.

terms.compare: Like the electricity that makes things move and respond.
terms.meaning: A programming language that makes pages interactive in the browser.
terms.more: Runs in the browser (frontend). Can react to taps, change the page, and talk to servers. Not related to Java.
terms.example: Image sliders and pop-up menus on the site use JavaScript.

terms.compare: Like writing a very exact recipe for a robot cook.
terms.meaning: Writing instructions a computer can follow.
terms.more: Code must be exact — computers don't guess what you meant.
terms.example: Editing functions.php is programming.

terms.compare: Like a labeled box where you keep something.
terms.meaning: A named place to store a value that can change.
terms.more: JavaScript: let name = 'Ana'; PHP: $name = 'Ana';
terms.example: WordPress uses variables like $post to hold the current post.

terms.compare: Like a recipe card you can use again and again.
terms.meaning: A named group of instructions you can run whenever needed.
terms.more: Functions can take inputs (parameters) and give back an output (return value).
terms.example: the_title() is a WordPress function that prints the post title.

terms.compare: Like stamping 100 envelopes, one by one, with the same stamp.
terms.meaning: Code that repeats until a job is done.
terms.more: Types: for, while, foreach. Careful: a loop that never stops freezes the program.
terms.example: "The Loop" in WordPress repeats to show each post.

terms.compare: Like an egg tray: many slots, each holding one thing, in order.
terms.meaning: A list of values stored together under one name.
terms.more: Items are numbered from 0. JavaScript: ['a','b','c']; PHP: array('a','b','c') or ['a','b','c'].
terms.example: A list of recent posts is often an array.

terms.compare: Like a typo in a recipe that makes the cake taste wrong.
terms.meaning: A mistake in code that makes it behave wrongly.
terms.more: Named after an actual moth found in an early computer in 1947.
terms.example: A plugin update that breaks the menu has a bug.

terms.compare: Like being a detective looking for why the cake tasted wrong.
terms.meaning: Finding and fixing bugs.
terms.more: Tools: error messages, logs, browser DevTools, WP_DEBUG in wp-config.php.
terms.example: Turning on WP_DEBUG shows PHP errors to help you debug.

terms.compare: Like an app you install on your phone to add a feature.
terms.meaning: An add-on that gives WordPress new features.
terms.more: Plugins are PHP code in wp-content/plugins. Too many or outdated plugins slow and endanger the site.
terms.example: Contact Form 7 or a backup plugin are examples.

terms.compare: Like the uniform and interior design of a store.
terms.meaning: A set of files that controls how a WordPress site looks.
terms.more: Made of PHP templates, CSS and JS in wp-content/themes. Use a child theme for your edits so updates don't erase them.
terms.example: Changing the theme changes the whole site's design.

terms.compare: Like keeping a ready-made batch of rice instead of cooking for every order.
terms.meaning: A saved copy of something so it loads faster next time.
terms.more: Browsers cache files; servers and plugins cache whole pages. Old cache can show outdated content — 'clear the cache'.
terms.example: If your edit doesn't appear, clear the browser or plugin cache.

terms.compare: Like photocopying important documents and keeping them in another drawer.
terms.meaning: A saved copy of files or data you can restore if something breaks.
terms.more: WordPress needs two parts backed up: the files AND the database. Test restoring sometimes.
terms.example: Always back up before updating WordPress or plugins.

terms.compare: Like a delivery truck carrying files between two buildings.
terms.meaning: A way to copy files between your computer and a server.
terms.more: FTP sends passwords unencrypted; SFTP or FTPS is the safe version. Tools: FileZilla, WinSCP.
terms.example: Uploading a theme folder to the server can be done with SFTP.

terms.compare: Like an alarm clock that reminds the computer to do a chore.
terms.meaning: A schedule that runs tasks automatically at set times.
terms.more: Cron is the Linux name. On Windows it's Task Scheduler. WordPress has its own 'WP-Cron' that runs when people visit.
terms.example: A nightly backup at 2 AM is a scheduled task.

terms.compare: Like a security guard at the gate checking who may come in.
terms.meaning: A system that allows or blocks network traffic based on rules.
terms.more: Can be hardware (in the network) or software (Windows Defender Firewall). Rules often mention ports and IPs.
terms.example: Opening port 443 in the firewall lets HTTPS visitors reach the server.

terms.compare: Like a restaurant menu: it lists what you can order and how.
terms.meaning: A defined way for one program to ask another program for data or actions.
terms.more: Application Programming Interface. Web APIs often send JSON over HTTP. WordPress has a REST API at /wp-json/.
terms.example: A plugin may use Google's API to show a map.

terms.compare: Like a neatly labeled form: name: Ana, age: 30.
terms.meaning: A simple text format for storing and sending data.
terms.more: JavaScript Object Notation. Example: {"name": "Ana", "age": 30}. This app's lessons are JSON files!
terms.example: WordPress REST API replies in JSON.

terms.compare: Like the dining area customers see.
terms.meaning: The part of a website you see and touch in the browser.
terms.more: Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
terms.example: The public pages of your site are the frontend.

terms.compare: Like the kitchen and storeroom customers don't see.
terms.meaning: The behind-the-scenes part: server, code and database.
terms.more: Built with languages like PHP plus a database. Also: the WordPress admin area is often called the backend.
terms.example: wp-admin and the MySQL database are the backend.

terms.compare: Like a ready-made house frame — you add walls and paint.
terms.meaning: A ready set of code and rules that speeds up building apps.
terms.more: Examples: Laravel (PHP), React (JavaScript), Bootstrap (CSS). This app uses no framework so you can see everything.
terms.example: Some themes are built on CSS frameworks like Bootstrap.

terms.compare: Like editions of a textbook: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.
terms.meaning: A numbered release of software.
terms.more: Often written as major.minor.patch, like 6.4.2. Big number changes can break things.
terms.example: Check the PHP version before installing a new plugin.

terms.compare: Like a save-game system: you can go back to any earlier save.
terms.meaning: A tool that tracks every change to your code so you can undo and compare.
terms.more: Each save is a 'commit'. Code can be shared online on GitHub.
terms.example: Keeping your child theme in Git lets you undo bad edits.

terms.compare: Like Google Drive, but for code saved with Git.
terms.meaning: A website that stores Git projects online and can host simple sites (GitHub Pages).
terms.more: GitHub Pages gives free HTTPS hosting for static sites like this app.
terms.example: You'll put TechBasics on GitHub Pages.

terms.compare: Like labels on boxes: 'This is a title', 'This is a paragraph'.
terms.meaning: An HTML marker in angle brackets that tells the browser what something is.
terms.more:
Most tags come in pairs:

opens,

closes. Some are single, like .
terms.example: The WordPress block editor creates tags for you behind the scenes.

terms.compare: Like one complete labeled box — label plus what's inside.
terms.meaning: An opening tag, its content and the closing tag together.
terms.more:
Hello

is one paragraph element. Elements can hold other elements (nesting).
terms.example: Each block in the WordPress editor becomes one or more elements.

terms.compare: Like extra details written on a box label: 'fragile', 'this side up'.
terms.meaning: Extra information inside an opening tag.
terms.more: Written as name="value". Example: or .
terms.example: Adding alt text to images in WordPress fills the alt attribute.

terms.compare: Like a teacher marking a document with 'title', 'note', 'important'.
terms.meaning: Text with tags added to describe its structure.
terms.more: HTML is a markup language — it marks parts, it doesn't calculate.
terms.example: When you switch the editor to 'Code', you see the markup.

terms.compare: Like a paper application form.
terms.meaning: Part of a page where visitors type and send information.
terms.more: Made with <form>, <input>, <label>, <button>. Data goes to the server via GET or POST.
terms.example: The agency's contact or feedback page uses a form.

terms.compare: Like water that takes the shape of any glass.
terms.meaning: A design that adjusts to any screen size.
terms.more: Uses flexible layouts and CSS media queries.
terms.example: Check that the agency site looks good on phones — that's responsive design.

terms.compare: Like a website that learned to behave like an app.
terms.meaning: A website that can be installed and work offline.
terms.more: Needs HTTPS, a manifest.json and a service worker. This app is a PWA!
terms.example: TechBasics on your Home Screen is a PWA.

terms.compare: Like a helper who keeps photocopies of everything in case the internet goes out.
terms.meaning: A background script that can save files for offline use.
terms.more: It sits between the app and the network and can answer from Cache Storage.
terms.example: Look at sw.js in this project — that's the service worker.

terms.compare: Like a TV remote for another computer far away.
terms.meaning: A way to see and control another computer over the network.
terms.more: Windows uses RDP on port 3389. Never leave it open to the whole internet.
terms.example: You may use Remote Desktop to manage the Windows server.

terms.compare: Like a ready-to-use store building where you just arrange shelves and products.
terms.meaning: A free system for building and managing websites without coding every page.
terms.more: A CMS (content management system) written in PHP with a MySQL database.
terms.example: Your agency's website runs on WordPress.

terms.compare: Like a bulletin-board manager who posts notices for you.
terms.meaning: Software that lets people manage website content without writing code.
terms.more: WordPress, Joomla and Drupal are CMSs.
terms.example: Staff post news through the WordPress CMS.

terms.compare: Like knocking on a door to see if anyone is home.
terms.meaning: A command that checks if another device can be reached and how fast.
terms.more: Run 'ping 8.8.8.8' in Command Prompt. It measures round-trip time in ms.
terms.example: Ping the server to check if it's online.

terms.compare: Like a recipe shared freely for anyone to use and improve.
terms.meaning: Software whose code is public and free to use and change.
terms.more: WordPress, PHP, Apache and MySQL are open source.
terms.example: Your whole website stack is mostly open source.

terms.compare: Like a word processor made especially for code.
terms.meaning: An app for writing code, with colors and helpful hints.
terms.more: Popular: Visual Studio Code (free). It colors tags and catches typos.
terms.example: Use VS Code to edit theme files instead of Notepad.

terms.compare: Like the line on a form that says 'This is Form 2026-A'.
terms.meaning: The first line of an HTML file that tells the browser 'this is modern HTML'.
terms.more: Written <!DOCTYPE html>. Without it browsers use old 'quirks' rules.
terms.example: Every WordPress theme's header.php starts the page with a DOCTYPE.

terms.compare: Like the back-office paperwork of a store — important but not on the shelves.
terms.meaning: The part of an HTML page with info about the page (title, styles), not shown as content.
terms.more: Holds <title>, <meta>, <link> to CSS, and some scripts.
terms.example: Plugins like Yoast add SEO tags into the <head>.

terms.compare: Like the store's display floor where customers walk.
terms.meaning: The part of an HTML page holding everything you see.
terms.more: Headings, paragraphs, images, links all go inside <body>.
terms.example: Your post content ends up somewhere inside <body>.

terms.compare: Like boxes inside boxes.
terms.meaning: Putting elements inside other elements.
terms.more:
Close inner tags before outer ones:

Hi

, not

Hi

.
terms.example: Broken nesting can mess up a page layout in WordPress.

terms.compare: Like a door from one room to another.
terms.meaning: Clickable text or image that takes you to another page.
terms.more: Made with text.
terms.example: Menu items in WordPress are hyperlinks.

terms.compare: Like describing a photo to a friend over the phone.
terms.meaning: A text description of an image for screen readers and when images fail to load.
terms.more: Written as alt="..." on . Important for accessibility and government web standards.
terms.example: Fill the 'Alternative Text' field when uploading images in WordPress.

terms.compare: Like adding ramps and braille signs to a building.
terms.meaning: Making websites usable by everyone, including people with disabilities.
terms.more: Good contrast, alt text, labels, keyboard support, headings in order.
terms.example: Government sites should be accessible to all citizens.

terms.compare: Like labeling rooms 'kitchen' and 'bedroom' instead of 'room 1' and 'room 2'.
terms.meaning: Using tags that describe meaning, like <nav>, <header>, <article>.
terms.more: Helps screen readers and search engines understand the page.
terms.example: Good WordPress themes use semantic tags.

terms.compare: Like putting a clear sign and directions so people can find your store.
terms.meaning: Making a site easy for search engines like Google to find and understand.
terms.more: Titles, headings, descriptions, fast pages and good links all help.
terms.example: An SEO plugin helps set page titles and descriptions.

terms.compare: Upload = sending a package out; download = receiving one.
terms.meaning: Upload: copy from your device to a server. Download: copy from a server to your device.
terms.more: Direction is always from YOUR point of view.
terms.example: Adding an image to the Media Library is an upload.

terms.compare: Like a security guard's logbook of who came and went.
terms.meaning: A file where programs write down what happened, including errors.
terms.more: IIS logs are in C:\inetpub\logs. PHP errors go to an error log.
terms.example: Check the logs when the site shows a white screen.
